findings.claim: "In Eduqas GCSE Music, AoS2 focuses on music written for small groups"; "assessed in the listening exam (Component 3)"
findings.truth: The board is never named to students, and the board's component code is not house vocabulary. Say "In AoS2" and "the listening exam".
findings.evidence: house rule (CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings; Eduqas/WJEC lessons never name the board)

findings.claim: "AoS2 is assessed via the listening exam only. ... One may focus on musical theatre or jazz, and the other on chamber music."
findings.truth: Knowledge of each area of study is tested in the listening exam (two questions per area), but a learner may also link the required ensemble performance and one of the four set composition briefs to AoS2. The spec never says which style each of the two questions takes; that split is invented.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 ("All learners are required to perform one ensemble piece and when this is linked to area of study 2 ..."), 2.2 (four briefs, one per area of study), 2.3 ("eight questions, two on each area of study")

findings.claim: "In the Autumn 2020 Eduqas exam, a chamber music extract was played and students were asked to identify the melody instrument (cello) ..."
findings.truth: Names the board and quotes a specific past paper. Describe the question type generically instead.
findings.evidence: house rule: board never named; no past-paper questions in any field

findings.claim: "Schoenberg’s “I Dreamed a Dream” from Les Misérables"
findings.truth: The composer of Les Misérables is Claude-Michel Schönberg. "Schoenberg" is the spelling used for Arnold Schoenberg, a different composer. Lesson 4 spells it correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Les Misérables (musical) / Claude-Michel Schönberg; L4 n38 of this unit

findings.claim: "The Eduqas spec requires you to identify and describe texture ... There are four main textures you must know" (monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, unison)
findings.truth: The area of study lists ten textures: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, unison, chordal, layered, melody and accompaniment, round, canon and countermelody. Telling a student four is the full list is a scope error. Also names the board.
findings.evidence: spec, Area of study 2: Music for Ensemble (texture list); Appendix C Texture list

findings.claim: "In the Autumn 2020 exam ... Answers that earned credit included: the melody was legato, diatonic, conjunct ..."
findings.truth: This is mark-scheme content from a named past paper. Teach the same features as guidance without citing the paper or the credit list.
findings.evidence: house rule: no mark-scheme indicative content in any field

findings.claim: "The Autumn 2020 paper included a question on a musical theatre extract ..."
findings.truth: Same past-paper citation. The musical fact (Tell Me It's Not True is from Blood Brothers by Willy Russell) is correct and is kept.
findings.evidence: house rule; Wikipedia: Blood Brothers (musical)

findings.claim: Card 4: q = "In the _____ 2020 Eduqas exam, a chamber music extract was played ... the performance technique (arco", a = "Autumn"
findings.truth: An auto-generated card cut off mid-sentence, testing an exam-series date rather than any music, and naming the board. Replaced with a texture card (monophonic), which duplicates no other answer in the lesson.
findings.evidence: house rule; validator rules on flashcards

findings.claim: Q3 labelled "4 marks" but the question sets "(a) Melody [3 marks] (b) Accompaniment [3 marks]" and the mark scheme awards any 3 + any 3
findings.truth: The question is worth 6 marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation from the question text and its own mark scheme

findings.claim: Q6 (a jazz ensemble question) labelled "12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score"
findings.truth: This area of study has no prepared extract. The exam sets two prepared extracts only, and they belong to the other two areas of study (a Bach flute movement and a 1982 pop song). A jazz question here is an unprepared extract.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Assessment of Component 3: "six will be on unprepared musical extracts and two on extracts set by WJEC"; the two prepared extracts are listed under areas of study 1 and 4

findings.claim: data-def for homophonic: "The combination of different musical layers sounding at the same time."
findings.truth: That defines texture in general. Homophonic is a main melody supported by chords, the parts often moving together in the same rhythm. Lesson 1 already defines it correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix C (Texture); L1 glossary of this unit

findings.claim: "elements of music" defined as melody, harmony, rhythm, dynamics, tempo, texture, timbre, articulation and structure
findings.truth: The examinable list of musical elements is melody, harmony, tonality, form and structure, dynamics, sonority, texture, tempo, rhythm and metre. Tonality, sonority and metre were missing.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Musical Elements list

findings.claim: Q2 ("State two instruments ...") labelled "1 mark" while its mark scheme says "1 mark each, 2 marks total"
findings.truth: The question is worth 2 marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation from its own mark scheme

findings.claim: "In the Eduqas GCSE Music exam, jazz and blues falls under AoS2"
findings.truth: The board is never named to students.
findings.evidence: house rule

findings.claim: Blues scale defined as "A six-note scale ... formed by adding flattened 3rd, 5th and 7th notes to a major scale" (repeated in the glossary, a flashcard and the takeaways)
findings.truth: Adding three flattened notes to a seven-note major scale cannot give six notes. The hexatonic blues scale is the MINOR pentatonic scale plus the flattened 5th: 1, ♭3, 4, ♭5, 5, ♭7. The lesson's own worked example (C, E♭, F, G♭, G, B♭) is that scale, so the definition contradicts the example. The flattened 3rd, 5th and 7th are the BLUE NOTES, which is a different idea.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Blues scale (hexatonic = minor pentatonic + ♭5); internal contradiction with n22 of this lesson

findings.claim: "The blues scale is built by taking the notes of a pentatonic scale and adding the flattened 5th", with pentatonic defined as "notes 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of the major scale"
findings.truth: That is the major pentatonic. Building on it gives C, D, E, G♭, G, A, not the scale the lesson then prints. The blues scale comes from the minor pentatonic (1, ♭3, 4, 5, ♭7). A student following this definition constructs the wrong scale.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Blues scale; Pentatonic scale

findings.claim: "Miles Davis – So What: A famous example of a jazz combo (trumpet, saxophone, piano, double bass, drums). Listen for the prominent bass line in the solo section"
findings.truth: The 1959 Kind of Blue recording is a sextet: Miles Davis (trumpet), Cannonball Adderley (alto sax), John Coltrane (tenor sax), Bill Evans (piano), Paul Chambers (double bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums). Two saxophones, not one. The notable feature is that the double bass states the head, not a bass line in the solos.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Kind of Blue (personnel); So What (Miles Davis composition)

findings.claim: Q2 ("State two features of the blues scale") labelled "1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer" with a max-2 mark scheme
findings.truth: It is a 2-mark short-answer question, not a 1-mark multiple choice.
findings.evidence: recomputation from its own mark scheme

findings.claim: Q3 ("Describe three typical features") labelled "4 marks" with a mark scheme capped at 3
findings.truth: The question is worth 3 marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation from its own mark scheme

findings.claim: "In Eduqas GCSE Music AoS2, musical theatre is one of the three ensemble types"
findings.truth: The board is never named to students.
findings.evidence: house rule

findings.claim: Section heading "Set Works You Should Know" over Defying Gravity, Prologue and I Dreamed a Dream; takeaway "Know the set examples"
findings.truth: This area of study sets no prepared extract and no set work. The exam sets two prepared extracts only, both in other areas of study. Calling these three songs set works tells a student to expect a printed score and a prepared-extract question that will never come.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Area of study 2 (no prepared extract listed, unlike areas of study 1 and 4); Assessment of Component 3

findings.claim: "If you choose a musical theatre brief for your free composition ..."
findings.truth: The area-of-study briefs are set by the board: learners pick one of four, one per area of study. The second composition is a FREE composition for which the learner writes their own brief. A musical theatre brief would be the set composition, not the free one.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Component 2 ("A composition which responds to a brief set by WJEC ... Learners select one from a choice of four briefs"; "A free composition ... Learners will set their own brief")

findings.claim: Q2 ("State two roles that the pit band performs") labelled "1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer" with a max-2 mark scheme
findings.truth: It is a 2-mark short-answer question.
findings.evidence: recomputation from its own mark scheme

findings.claim: Q3 ("Describe three ways ...") labelled "4 marks" with a mark scheme capped at 3
findings.truth: The question is worth 3 marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation from its own mark scheme

findings.claim: Q6, a written comparison of musical theatre and chamber music, labelled "12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)"
findings.truth: No extract is played and this area of study has no prepared extract. The label promises a question format that does not exist here.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Assessment of Component 3

findings.claim: "Quality of written communication assessed." (L4 Q6) and "Indicative content (QWC assessed — quality of written communication)" (L3 Q6)
findings.truth: This specification awards no marks for quality of written communication or SPaG anywhere. The word does not appear in the spec. Telling a student their writing quality is marked is a false exam claim.
findings.evidence: spec grep: no SPaG, no "quality of written communication"; assessment objectives are AO1-AO4 only

findings.claim: Q4 and Q5 labelled "10 marks — Extended Listening Response" but each mark scheme opens "Award marks for relevant, well-explained points using musical vocabulary (up to 4 marks)"
findings.truth: The ceiling should be 10 marks; each scheme already lists six to seven creditable points.
findings.evidence: recomputation against the question label and the point list

findings.claim: Q5's mark scheme prints a five-rung ladder of band descriptors ("9–10: Perceptive answer with detailed explanation ... Accurate specialist vocabulary", down to "0: No relevant information")
findings.truth: Two options. Either rewrite the ladder in house band names (Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band) with house wording, as lessons 3 and 4 of this unit already do, or drop the ladder and keep only the indicative content. The wording reads close to a board mark scheme (perceptive / critical judgements / specialist vocabulary), which the copyright-distancing rule forbids. Recommendation: rewrite in the house ladder to match the rest of the unit. Not edited here because the band-ladder sweep is a separate fleet-wide workstream.
findings.evidence: house rule on mark-scheme descriptors; L3 Q5-Q6 and L4 Q6 of this unit already use Top/Mid/Lower band

findings.claim: "In Bessie Smith's Lost Your Head Blues, the vocal line sings a phrase (the call) and the trumpet answers"
findings.truth: The record was cut on 4 May 1926 with Joe Smith on the obbligato. He is usually credited as a cornetist on the Bessie Smith sessions, though sources also describe him as a trumpeter. Not settled enough to correct; the call-and-response point is right either way.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Bessie Smith (discography date); Joe Smith (musician) — article says trumpet in the text and "her preferred cornetist" in the quote

findings.claim: Several data-revision-tip attributes are cut off mid-sentence, e.g. "Cover this box. Write down what you recall about jazz, the rhythm section (piano, bass." (L1 n19), "Define in a big band, the melody in your own words." (L2 n34), "Write down what you recall about jazz and blues music commonly uses swung." (L3 n4)
findings.truth: Auto-generated tips truncated at a fixed length. Not a factual error, so left alone, but a student sees them on the revision-tip control.
findings.evidence: raw content of L1, L2, L3

findings.claim: "Chamber music is purely instrumental and focuses on abstract musical ideas."
findings.truth: Vocal chamber music exists, and this area of study names vocal ensembles among its groupings. The line is a fair GCSE simplification in a comparison with musical theatre, so it is not corrected.
findings.evidence: spec, Area of study 2 groupings list (vocal ensembles)

summary: All four lessons carry findings. The worst are a blues scale built from the wrong pentatonic (lesson 3, in four places, contradicting the lesson's own worked example), musical theatre songs taught as 'set works' when this area of study sets no prepared extract (lesson 4, plus a matching 12-mark 'Prepared Extract with Score' label in lessons 1 and 4), the board named in prose in lessons 1, 3 and 4 with two past-paper citations, and nine practice questions whose mark label contradicts their own mark scheme.
